content: The ampere, commonly referred to as amp (symbol: A), is the unit of electric current, which quantifies the amount of electric charge passing a point per second. It is one of the seven base units in the International System of Units (SI) and is named after André-Marie Ampère, a key figure in the discovery of electromagnetism. The ampere is defined as the constant current that, if maintained in two straight, parallel conductors of infinite length and negligible circular cross-section, placed one meter apart in a vacuum, would produce a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ newtons per meter of length between these conductors. This definition is rooted in Ampère's force law, which describes the interaction between electric currents. The ampere is a fundamental SI base unit, alongside the meter, kilogram, second, kelvin, mole, and candela. It is defined independently of the quantity of electric charge. The unit of electric charge, the coulomb, is derived from the ampere and is defined as the amount of charge displaced by a one-ampere current in one second. Conversely, one ampere corresponds to one coulomb of charge passing a given point in one second. Mathematically, the relationship between charge (Q), current (I), and time (t) is expressed as Q = I × t. The most precise realization of the ampere is achieved using a watt balance, but in practice, it is maintained through Ohm's Law, which relates the units of electromotive force (volts) and resistance (ohms). These units are tied to reproducible physical phenomena, specifically the Josephson junction for voltage and the quantum Hall effect for resistance. The official realization of the standard ampere is detailed in NIST Special Publication 330. It is based on the movement of 1/(1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹) elementary charges (such as electrons) per second, which corresponds to approximately 6.241509074 × 10¹⁸ charges per second. Proposals have been made to redefine the kilogram and other SI base units in terms of fixed values of fundamental physical constants. One such proposal defines the kilogram as the mass that would be accelerated at precisely 2 × 10⁻⁷ m/s² when subjected to the force per meter between two parallel conductors, one meter apart in a vacuum, carrying a constant current of exactly 6.241509479607717888 × 10¹⁸ elementary charges per second. This would result in a consistent definition of the coulomb as the total of exactly 6.241509479607717888 × 10¹⁸ elementary charges and the ampere as the current corresponding to this flow of charges per second.
